summary: This program stores two true/false values in boolean variables, prints them, and then combines them with logical operators to produce a third boolean. It shows that boolean values can be computed and displayed like any other data, without needing an if statement.

lines.text: A boolean variable holds only one of two values, true or false. Note that true is a Java keyword, not the text "true" in quotes.
The second boolean starts out false, which will matter when the two are combined below.
When a boolean is joined to a string with +, Java automatically converts it to the words true or false for display.
The && operator yields true only when both sides are true, and ! flips a boolean to its opposite. So this reads as "Java is fun and there are no bugs," which works out to true.
Printing the computed result shows that logical expressions produce a boolean value you can store and reuse, with no conditional statement involved.
